# Typhus carried by body lice (delousing) (`typhus_lice`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/medicine.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Medicine & hygiene (`medicine`)
- Deps: helped by contagion_theory, soap, military_camp_hygiene, heat_sterilisation
- Core idea: Epidemic typhus, the fever of armies, jails, ships and famines, is usually spread by body lice. These live and lay their eggs in the seams of clothing and bedding, not on the skin, and the disease enters when their droppings are scratched into the skin. Epidemic typhus can also recur years after the original infection. Delouse everyone in a group on the same day: wash the body with soap, cut or comb the hair, and boil all clothes and bedding for ten minutes, or bake them in an oven at about the heat for bread once the bread is out, or press the seams with a hot iron. Repeat weekly. Clothes left unworn for two to three weeks are free of lice. New arrivals are washed and their clothes baked before they join the others.
- Pitfalls:
  - Washing the person but putting the same clothes back on; the lice are in the seams
  - Washing clothes in cold or lukewarm water, which lice and eggs survive
  - Confusing body lice with head lice, or typhus with typhoid
  - Blaming rats; rat fleas carry the milder murine typhus, not the epidemic kind
  - Deloused people sharing blankets and straw with those not yet treated
- History: europe: 1489–1490 – first clearly described epidemic, siege of Granada; 1546 Fracastoro separates typhus from plague; 1750s–1760s Pringle and Lind have recruits stripped and washed and their clothes baked, on a theory of infected clothing; 1812 typhus destroys much of Napoleon's army in Russia; africa: 1909 – Nicolle in Tunis proves transmission by the body louse (patients stop infecting others once washed and reclothed); global: 1915 Serbia and 1918–1922 Russia – millions of cases; 1930s Weigl and Cox vaccines; 1943–1944 DDT dusting ends the Naples epidemic
- Read:
  - Charles Nicolle, C. Comte and E. Conseil, Transmission expérimentale du typhus exanthématique par le pou du corps, Comptes rendus de l'Académie des Sciences (1909)
  - Hans Zinsser, Rats, Lice and History (1935)
